title: Exposure Response Desk for Vibe-Coded Apps
one_liner: A fix-and-legal-decision service for founders whose AI-built apps leaked user data, delivering an RLS lockdown, an access-log check and a breach-notification memo.
customer: Non-technical founders and small businesses that shipped apps on Lovable, Bolt, Replit or Cursor with a Supabase backend, and small agencies that build such apps for local clients. They pay $149-$499 per incident plus $29/month monitoring.
problem: On Sept 25, 2026 UpGuard reported about 16,000 Supabase databases publicly exposing names, home addresses, phone numbers, passwords, auth tokens, private conversations and license plate records. AI coding tools write SQL migrations where Row-Level Security defaults to off, and founders never turn it on. An earlier flaw, CVE-2025-48757, exposed 170+ Lovable apps. Owners do not know how to fix it without breaking the app, whether anyone actually accessed the data, or whether they now have a legal duty to notify users and regulators.
solution: Not another scanner, since ShipSafe and VibeAppScanner already exist. This is a response desk. (1) The owner authorizes a read-only check on their own project. (2) The tool generates and tests an RLS policy pull request for common patterns (owner-only rows, public read and owner write, storage buckets) that does not break the app. (3) It reviews available Supabase API and Postgres logs to estimate whether anonymous-key access from unknown sources occurred. (4) A partner privacy attorney's state-by-state and GDPR decision tree produces a notification-or-not memo. (5) It drafts user notices and an evidence packet for the owner's cyber insurer. Continuous monitoring is upsell.
why_now: The UpGuard disclosure is three days old, and Cursor AI is the fastest-growing Glimpse trend of 2026 (+2,213%), with Cyber Insurance up 763% on Exploding Topics. Mass disclosures of this kind will keep recurring as more founders ship AI-built apps. Legal clocks (GDPR 72 hours, state laws with 30-60 day windows) create urgency at exactly the moment the owner learns of the exposure.
revenue_model: $149 lockdown-only tier, $499 lockdown plus log review plus notification memo and letters, $29/month continuous monitoring, and $99/client wholesale packages for agencies. Later: referral fees from cyber insurers and privacy counsel.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone sells detection. Nobody sells the 'now what', and the mission-critical question for an owner is legal, not technical. The trigger is public and fresh: UpGuard found ~16,000 exposed Supabase databases, the root cause is that AI-written migrations leave RLS off, and Supabase's CISO says security 'ultimately remains a shared responsibility' (https://startupfortune.com/upguard-found-16000-supabase-databases-leaking-user-data-to-the-open-web/). CVE-2025-48757 previously exposed 170+ Lovable apps, and the common failure is founders who cannot debug RLS (https://www.superblocks.com/blog/lovable-vulnerabilities). The scanner market already exists (https://vibeappscanner.com/lovable-security), which means paid demand is proven while the response step remains unowned. Cursor AI's +2,213% growth is the #1 item at https://meetglimpse.com/trends/.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: build the read-only exposure checker that owners run on their own project, plus an RLS policy generator for the five most common patterns. Days 8-15: co-author a 'Supabase RLS was off, what now? (24-hour plan)' guide with a privacy attorney and publish it for SEO and Reddit (r/lovable, r/supabase, Indie Hackers). Days 16-30: sell 20 lockdown fixes at $149-$199 and sign 2 small agencies at wholesale rates. Skip scanning anyone's databases without their authorization.

title: Executor-of-Last-Resort for Solo Agers
one_liner: A subscription that names a licensed fiduciary as your executor and runs daily wellness checks, so a childless retiree isn't found weeks late and handed to a court-appointed stranger.
customer: Unpartnered or childless adults 65+ with $100K-$1.5M estates (too small for most corporate trustees, too large to ignore), plus their elder-law attorneys, senior living communities and Area Agencies on Aging.
problem: Solo agers have no obvious executor, agent or emergency contact, and named friends or nieces often flake. Japan shows the downstream effect: 37,227 people living alone were found dead at home in H1 2024, nearly 4,000 undiscovered for over a month. The US has no equivalent service layer, and intestate estates go to public administrators.
solution: A 'Stewardship Plan'. (a) A licensed professional fiduciary or trust company partner agrees to serve as successor agent and executor. (b) Passive wellness signals (phone, smart speaker, utility use, optional wearable) plus a daily automated or human check-in escalate to neighbors and welfare checks. (c) A digital go-bag holds accounts, medications, pets, keys and funeral wishes. (d) At death it triggers funeral instructions, securing the house, clear-out and estate administration for a fee schedule.
why_now: Cheap ambient signals and voice-AI check-in calls make monitoring inexpensive. Death care is proving roll-up-able (Everstory, SCI), yet no one serves the years before death for people without heirs. Estates and consolidator data show volume is flat, so services attached to existing customers are where growth sits.
revenue_model: $39-$79/month subscription, executor fees at death (often statutory, a few percent of the estate), margin on clear-out and estate services, and B2B fees from senior living and AAAs.
non_obvious_insight: The first customer isn't dying. She is buying certainty that someone competent shows up on the worst day. Subscriptions fund the acquisition of a low-cost executor book that pays out later.
first_30_days: Partner with a licensed fiduciary in one state. Sign 3 elder-law attorneys. Recruit a 30-person waitlist through senior centers and 'elder orphan' groups. Charge $99 setup plus $49/month and run the daily check-in calls manually at first.

title: Launch and Reentry Airspace Forecasts for Airlines
one_liner: A dispatcher-facing forecast of whether launch and debris closures will really happen, and what rerouting will cost.
customer: Airline operations control centers on Caribbean, Atlantic and Pacific routes, cargo airlines, business-jet operators and flight-planning software vendors.
problem: Launches hit 321 in 2025, and Starship debris in early 2025 disrupted flights around Florida and the Caribbean. Launch slips and scrubs make late notices unreliable. Dispatchers over-buffer fuel and time or get surprised, and there is no probabilistic view of hazard areas.
solution: An API and dashboard that fuses launch manifests, vehicle-specific slip and scrub statistics, trajectory and debris-response-area models, and reentry predictions. It outputs closure probability and expected reroute cost per flight. Deliver it into existing flight-planning tools as a plug-in.
why_now: Cadence is climbing (223 launches in 2023 to 321 in 2025), Starship is flying orbital profiles, and new vehicles such as New Glenn and Stoke's Nova are coming. Airspace impact scales with cadence.
revenue_model: $30-150k per year per airline. Per-flight API fees through flight-planning vendors. Cargo and charter tiers.
non_obvious_insight: The valuable prediction is not where the hazard area is but whether the launch will actually go, which is a schedule-slip model. That converts publicly available manifests into a decision-quality product.
first_30_days: Backtest a slip and scrub model on the last 12 months of Florida and Vandenberg launches. Show it to five dispatch managers at airlines flying Caribbean routes. Offer a free pilot on one route and a paid tier for the next quarter.

title: Transfer-Portal Durability Passport for College Athletes
one_liner: An athlete-owned, verified injury and load history that programs will demand before they commit six figures of revenue share.
customer: College programs (general managers, sports medicine, compliance), collectives and agents pay for verified dossiers; athletes get their file free and own it.
problem: Chain: the House settlement lets schools pay athletes up to about $20.5M in 2025-26, unlimited transfers and the June 2026 shift to a five-year eligibility clock make multi-year, money-bearing roster bets, yet there is no standard electronic medical record across schools. Injury history moves by phone call and rumor: athletes fear disclosure, programs fear buying a torn ACL, and agents cannot prove durability.
solution: A consent-based portal where athletes' athletic trainers upload structured injury and return-to-play summaries, a standardized functional battery (jump/landing, isometric strength, hop tests) run at partner performance gyms, and optional load history exports from Catapult or WHOOP. The athlete chooses who sees what; the receiving program pays for a standardized, verified dossier.
why_now: Revenue-share contracts, unlimited transfers and the 2026 eligibility overhaul raise the financial stakes of injuries; the proposed Protect College Sports Act would add post-eligibility medical coverage duties and privacy protections; state privacy laws and HIPRA push consent-based data handling.
revenue_model: $150-300 per verified passport paid by the receiving program; $10-25k per year per program for scouting and post-signing baselines; $99 per athlete from agents.
non_obvious_insight: The athlete, not the school, must own the file: that is what makes disclosure acceptable and gives buyers something they can trust. It is a Carfax for players, and the customers now have real money at risk.
first_30_days: Recruit 30 mid-major and D2 basketball and volleyball athletes entering the portal through 3-4 friendly agents, build the consent form and one-page dossier, run 10 test sessions at a local performance gym, and pitch three assistant coaches or GMs on paying $200 per dossier.

title: Buy the Restaurant Alley: Used-Oil Route Roll-Up
one_liner: Consolidate small used-cooking-oil haulers into one AI-run route business, then sell every other mandated back-of-restaurant service from the same truck.
customer: Independent restaurants and small chains (who now get paid for their oil and buy add-on services), renewable diesel and SAF refiners buying traceable domestic feedstock, and retiring collector owners selling their routes.
problem: From 2026 the 45Z clean-fuel credit applies only to North American feedstock, and UCO prices have run at roughly $1,000 to $1,400 per tonne. Restaurants historically gave oil away under auto-renewing contracts with big renderers, and theft is common. Small collectors lack chain-of-custody paperwork and contamination grading, and refiners want traceable domestic supply.
solution: Acquire 8 to 15 small collectors, grease-trap pumpers and hood cleaners in one metro. AI ops: fill-level sensors or photo estimates to cut truck miles 25% to 40%, vision-based contamination grading at pickup, automatic chain-of-custody and sustainability documentation for refiners, and a contract-reading agent that finds competitors' termination windows and times win-back offers. Add hood cleaning, grease-trap pumping and fire-suppression inspection on the same route visits.
why_now: 45Z limits credits to North American feedstock from 2026, which makes domestic UCO scarce and valuable, and documentation that used to be optional is now a selling point. Owners of small routes are aging out, and route-optimization and photo-grading tools are cheap.
revenue_model: Spread on oil resale to refiners with a share paid to restaurants, plus $150 to $500 per add-on service visit, plus a traceability premium from refiners.
non_obvious_insight: The real asset isn't the trucks; it's the contract calendar. Thousands of evergreen grease agreements with 30 to 90 day cancellation windows can be read, mapped and timed. The alley visit is also the cheapest customer touchpoint for every other mandated back-of-house service.
first_30_days: Approach a retiring one-truck collector about a seller-financed purchase in the $200k to $600k range, or start as a broker with a subcontracted truck offering 20 to 30 restaurants a paid pickup. Build a photo-based intake and contract tracker. Target franchisee groups with 5 to 10 units. Pre-sell forward oil volume to a regional biodiesel or renewable diesel refiner using documented chain of custody.

title: After-Death Home Reset for Hospice Families
one_liner: A two-person crew that returns the house to normal within 48 hours of a home hospice death: bed out, meds destroyed, room restored, memory box packed.
customer: Hospice agencies pay per home death, as a family-experience and bereavement differentiator. A second stream is families paying a premium, and funeral homes reselling it as an add-on.
problem: After a home death the hospital bed, oxygen concentrator and commode often sit in the living room for days. The DME vendor schedules pickup on its own clock. The leftover morphine, lorazepam and haloperidol 'comfort kit' sits in the fridge or cabinet. Nurses are supposed to see to disposal, but the home visit is often skipped or rushed, and families quietly keep or mis-dispose of them. The dead person's glasses, dentures and hearing aids end up in a drawer. The family remembers the empty bed in the middle of the room for the rest of their lives. The CAHPS Hospice family survey arrives months later and those last impressions color the answers.
solution: A chaplain-designed protocol delivered by two trained, background-checked staff in a branded van. On admission, the hospice photographs the room so the crew can restore the original furniture layout. Within 24 to 48 hours of death the crew coordinates or performs bed and equipment removal, destroys leftover controlled drugs with deactivation pouches and a witnessed log the hospice can put in the chart, and launders linens. They pack a memory box (glasses, jewelry, a worn shirt, the last handwritten note). They restore the room, open the windows, and offer a two-minute optional blessing or silence. A hand-off card tells the family what happens at 2 weeks and 6 weeks.
why_now: Hospice is consolidating, with private equity and large chains competing on public CAHPS-based quality scores that drive referrals. Regulators and communities are paying more attention to opioid diversion. Hospice per-diem margins are squeezed and the DME vendors they use are getting slower and cheaper. Home is where most hospice deaths occur. Also, nurses are stretched thin, so the care they used to give informally in that first day is disappearing, and nobody owns it.
revenue_model: Hospice pays $250 to $400 per home death on a per-case contract, with volume tiers. Families or funeral homes pay $450 to $600 for a premium version with a full room refresh and donation pickup for clothing and mobility aids. A hospice with roughly 100 patients on service has on the order of 25 to 35 deaths a month, around half at home, so three hospices support a small crew. Sponsorship from a nonprofit hospice foundation can cover indigent families.
non_obvious_insight: Outsiders think the crisis is the moment of death. Insiders know the emotional injury persists in the physical room and in the loose ends nobody owns: the bed, the drugs, the dentures. The hospice would love to solve it but cannot bill for it and the nurse has already left. Whoever owns hours 6 through 48 after death, when the funeral home has taken the body and all clinical staff have gone, owns the family's memory of the hospice.
first_30_days: Sign one small nonprofit hospice as a design partner. Write the checklist with the chaplain, the DON and a pharmacist for the controlled-drug disposal log. Buy a used van, get general liability coverage, and hire two people with home-health-aide or hospitality backgrounds. Do the first 5 to 8 resets free in exchange for family feedback. Charge from case 9, and ask the hospice's quality director to compare family feedback scores with and without the reset.

title: Model-of-Origin Forensics for AI Music Catalogs
one_liner: Attribute a track to the generator and version that made it, so catalog owners and litigators can separate legacy unlicensed-model output from the rest.
customer: Distributors, sync and production-music libraries, entertainment law firms and insurers, plus brand legal teams clearing ad music.
problem: Suno replaced its models on Sep 9 with one trained on licensed music, after label suits. A second UMG/Sony suit over roughly 60k songs is reported (single source, verify). Warner settled. Tens of millions of tracks from older models are already distributed or embedded in videos and ads. Downstream legal exposure is unproven, but risk-averse counsel will want to know which tracks came from which model. Deezer's detector answers 'AI or not,' and is licensed only to platforms.
solution: A classifier and evidence report attributing audio to a generator family and version range (Suno, Udio, Stable Audio, ElevenLabs Music and others), trained on labeled corpora we generate ourselves from paid subscriptions to each version. Output: family, version range, confidence, and whether a post-Aug 6 Suno watermark is present. Includes catalog-level exposure heat maps, a batch API, and expert-witness-ready reports.
why_now: Suno's Sep 9 model swap and Aug 6 watermarking pledge create a hard before-and-after line. Pre-watermark, pre-swap tracks are exactly the legacy tail that needs forensic attribution, and the lawsuits make the question urgent.
revenue_model: $0.05-0.25 per track for batch screening, $5-50k per catalog audit, $15-75k per litigation-grade report, and annual retainers for law firms and insurers.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone is building 'AI or not' detectors, which are crowded and sell at consumer prices ($20/month). Nobody sells 'which model, which version, before or after the licensed swap.' That is the question that maps to legal liability, so it prices like legal risk.
first_30_days: Subscribe to the major generators and produce about 5k labeled tracks per version. Get a baseline classifier working in three weeks. Approach five sync libraries and two boutique entertainment-law firms, and sell $10k pilot audits of a 20k-track catalog subset.

title: Convert Empty Thai Hotel Floors to Monthly Stays
one_liner: Take under-filled floors of mid-tier Thai hotels on revenue share and run them as furnished 30-90 day remote-worker wings, replacing lost Chinese group demand with sticky monthly stays.
customer: Owners of 80-300 room three- and four-star hotels in Bangkok, Phuket, Pattaya and Chiang Mai whose Chinese group volume collapsed. End users are remote workers, retirees and long-stay sports or wellness visitors.
problem: Thailand's 2025 arrivals fell 7.2% and sit 17% below 2019, with Chinese arrivals down 33.5%. Insiders wait for Chinese groups to return, but Chinese outbound is shifting to independent travellers who go farther and spend less on hotels. Empty floors bleed fixed costs, while nomads on 40+ visa schemes struggle to find reliable monthly stays.
solution: We take 20-40% of rooms and add a coworking corner, bonded fast internet, laundry, community events and monthly billing. Guests pay USD 650-1,100 per month including utilities, for a 30-day minimum. We market through nomad communities and groups and help with long-stay visa paperwork. The hotel keeps F&B upside.
why_now: The China demand collapse leaves stranded capacity. Thailand's long-stay Destination Thailand Visa exists for remote workers, and 40+ countries now offer nomad visas. Nomad information is now free (Nomads.com sells lifetime membership for USD 1), so operators win on product, not discovery.
revenue_model: A 20-30% management fee on room revenue or a fixed lease spread, plus ancillary revenue from SIMs, insurance and visa-service referrals.
non_obvious_insight: Hotels are optimised for nights while nomads buy months. A floor at 90% occupancy on monthly rates beats 35% occupancy at full nightly rates, and monthly guests do not pay 22-28% OTA commission.
first_30_days: Sign 2 hotels in Bangkok or Chiang Mai on a 60-day trial of 10 rooms each. Build a one-page site and post in nomad and expat groups. Target 15 monthly bookings, and record occupancy and revenue per available room against the hotel's nightly baseline.

title: Landlord Loan Radar for Office Tenants
one_liner: Monitoring and lease-audit software that warns small office tenants when their landlord's loan is heading for trouble and recovers overbilled operating expenses.
customer: Tenants of 3,000-40,000 sf in office buildings (law, accounting, medical, nonprofit), their tenant-rep brokers, and office managers.
problem: With 17.8% national vacancy, 13.2% office CMBS delinquency and $39B maturing in a year, tenants sign renewals blind to the landlord's debt cliff. Distressed landlords may stop funding improvements or cut services, and operating-expense pass-throughs (gross-up, admin-fee caps, capital items) are often mis-billed, especially at low occupancy. Only large tenants can afford audit consultants.
solution: Public CMBS loan-level filings feed a radar that alerts on maturity dates, DSCR or occupancy drops and special-servicing transfers. An opex audit takes a lease and annual reconciliation and flags gross-up and base-year errors and non-recoverable capital costs. A 'renewal leverage brief' shows when the landlord needs an extension to refinance.
why_now: Elevated vacancy gives tenants leverage, distress is at a multi-year high, and document-reading software makes small-lease audits economical.
revenue_model: $149-299 per month per lease for monitoring, 25-30% success fee on recovered overbilling, and a white-label version for tenant-rep brokers.
non_obvious_insight: The landlord's refinancing deadline is public but nobody reads it, and a lease extension is exactly what a lender wants to see. A tenant who knows this can trade a signature for concessions.
first_30_days: Build a watchlist for three metros from public CMBS filings. Offer a free 'is your building on the list' checker and email 500 small firms in those buildings. Sell success-fee audits to the first five responders.

title: Telemetry-Underwritten Credit for Defense Sub-Tier Shops
angle: Pairing 2: Reshoring, tariffs & automation x Government / defense / municipal
one_liner: Plug low-cost MTConnect adapters into shop CNC machines to create tamper-evident proof of utilization and surge capacity that unlocks equipment loans and rated-order credit lines, and gives primes the capacity data they lack.
customer: 10-50 person machine shops, foundries and sheet-metal shops pursuing defense work (they pay $149-299 a month). Lenders, CDFIs and equipment lessors pay origination fees, and primes and state defense-industrial-base offices later pay for verified-capacity queries.
problem: An industry study finds 'no fit-for-purpose investment model' between R&D and mature production for sub-tier suppliers (castings, forgings, sensors, rocket motors), with VC a sliver and PE putting in only $1-3B a year. Hadrian raised $1.37B while metals robot orders rose just 3% in H1, and shops cannot fund a machine or a cobot cell. Lenders underwrite job shops on tax returns and collateral, and DoD has no real-time data on free spindle-hours.
solution: A hardware-light MTConnect and OPC UA adapter kit and cloud service that logs spindle utilization, part counts, scrap and on-time delivery with signed, tamper-evident records. It issues a 'verified capacity score', lender-ready utilization letters and attestations for DPAS-rated orders, and an anonymized open-capacity feed for primes and government. Partner lenders extend equipment loans and rated-order lines against the score.
why_now: Rated orders, drone and munitions surges and Navy co-investment are pushing demand to sub-tiers just as the Navy stops funding early stages. Publicly funded defense-industrial-base lending vehicles need originators. Modern CNC controls already speak MTConnect, so the marginal hardware cost is small.
revenue_model: $149-299 a month per shop for telemetry and score, 1-2% origination fee from lenders on funded loans, and later a per-query fee from primes and agencies for verified surge capacity.
non_obvious_insight: Utilization telemetry is a better credit signal than a tax return for a job shop, and it doubles as the surge-capacity data the government has never had. The same tamper-evident record serves the lender, the prime and the auditor, so shops pay because it gets them financed.
first_30_days: Partner with a manufacturing extension center and one CDFI or equipment lessor. Install adapters on 10 machines in a defense-heavy cluster (Connecticut or Ohio) and produce the first 3 verified utilization letters to test whether a lender will price better against them.

title: Youth Clubs as the Ban-Proof Group Chat
one_liner: A roster-anchored messaging layer for sports leagues, scout councils and youth groups that reuses the club's adult-verified roster as a safe, auditable chat for 9-15 year olds, paid by the club.
customer: Regional youth sports leagues, scout councils, robotics/FIRST teams and church youth groups (5k-100k members), plus their liability insurers. Parents use it free.
problem: Under-16 bans (Australia, Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, several US states) push kids into private chats and games. Everyone's answer is a new 'safe social network for kids', which dies on cold start. Meanwhile clubs already hold the verified network (background-checked coaches, rosters, parent contacts) but run it on WhatsApp, GroupMe and Snap groups with coach-to-child DMs. Youth-safety policies such as SafeSport's (from memory) prohibit exactly those DMs, and leagues cannot audit them.
solution: Team and league chats built on the registration data the club already has (DOB, parent identity). No one-to-one adult-minor DMs unless a second guardian is copied. Kid accounts are age-tiered and parent-linked, with no discovery, ads or strangers. Keyword flags go to the club safety officer. An exportable audit log goes to the insurer. Kids age out into open platforms at 16.
why_now: Ban leakage (VPNs under A$20 a month, 75% of Australian teens planning to stay on) means kids need somewhere else to talk. Insurers are tightening abuse-and-molestation coverage (from memory). Fall registration season is happening now, so the product can ride the season's registration fee.
revenue_model: $1-4 per member per season, bundled into the league's registration fee. Enterprise licence for councils. Referral fees or premium credits from insurers.
non_obvious_insight: The hard part of safe kids' social is distribution and verification, not software. A club has the graph, the identity check, a legal duty of care and a budget, and nobody has packaged that.
first_30_days: Interview 15 league directors and two youth-sports insurers. Ship a white-label chat on Stream or Sendbird for two leagues in one metro. Sell it as 'audit-ready coach-athlete messaging' at $1 per kid during fall registration. Collect an insurer endorsement or premium-credit letter.

title: Recertified Used Transformer Exchange
one_liner: A test-and-warranty marketplace that turns utility-retired transformers into energizable supply for data centers, solar and storage projects, instead of scrap.
customer: Data-center developers, solar and BESS EPCs, rural co-ops and industrial plants (buyers), sourcing from utility surplus desks and scrap dealers.
problem: AI data centers, solar, storage and grid upgrades have stretched transformer lead times to years, and tariffs on imported electrical steel and equipment make it worse. Meanwhile serviceable retired units are sold to scrap dealers priced by weight, worth a small fraction of a working unit.
solution: Buy or consign retired pad-mount and small substation units, run a standard test protocol (turns ratio, winding resistance, insulation, oil dissolved-gas analysis, PCB screening), refurbish through partner shops, and warrant them for 1-3 years. Units that fail go to core (grain-oriented steel) and copper recovery.
why_now: Transformer scarcity is the 2025-26 gating item for energization across data centers and solar/BESS. Tariffs on steel and derivatives raise new-unit prices, and developers are now willing to pay for schedule certainty.
revenue_model: 10-20% margin or commission ($3-15K per unit), plus $2-5K test and certification fees.
non_obvious_insight: Scrap yards price transformers by weight, while buyers price them by lead time. The arbitrage is a test-and-warranty product, not hardware. The trust layer includes PCB screening, which incumbents avoid.
first_30_days: Sign 3 scrap dealers or utility surplus contacts and contract a test lab. List 20 units with spec sheets. Approach 5 solar and BESS EPCs with schedule pain and close 2 paid pilots.

title: Drone-Ready Rx Lockers as Adherence Infrastructure
angle: Pairing 1: Aging/silver economy x Logistics & physical automation
one_liner: A lockable, temperature-buffered, authenticated receiving station at a senior's home that accepts drone or courier drops and quietly reports whether the medication was retrieved.
customer: Medicare Advantage plans and pharmacy chains, paying per active station plus per delivery. Independent-living communities are the pilot channel.
problem: Drone delivery is scaling (Wing/Walmart 270+ sites by 2027, Lowe's launch on Sep 28, 2026), but a 78-year-old cannot reliably receive a 2.5 lb drop. Bending, theft, weather and controlled-substance rules get in the way. Plans lose Star Ratings money on medication non-adherence, and solo agers have no daily check-in.
solution: A roughly $120 bill-of-materials box (porch, balcony or window mounted) with recipient authentication, insulation and a retrieval sensor. Start with human courier deliveries into the same locker, and add drone-network integration as it opens. A missed-retrieval alert goes to the pharmacy, then the family.
why_now: Retail drone networks are now big enough to need a receiving standard. Part D adherence measures are triple-weighted in Star Ratings. Medicare Advantage benefit cuts (OTC benefits from 9.6% to 2.4% of plans) push plans to look for outcome-linked spend.
revenue_model: $8-15 per month per station from plans or pharmacies, plus a per-retrieval fee to drone operators or pharmacies. Optional hardware financing.
non_obvious_insight: The delivery event is the cheapest, least creepy daily proof-of-life signal, and no camera or wearable is needed. The receiving end, not the flight, is the missing piece of senior drone delivery.
first_30_days: Build 20 units. Place them in two independent-living communities where the operator controls the landing zone. Sign an independent pharmacy chain for human-courier deliveries. Bring adherence and retrieval data to one MA plan's pharmacy team.

title: Collections That Hunt the Payer, Not the Patient
one_liner: A contingency-fee receivables firm for ambulance agencies and ER physician groups that, within 30 days of a self-pay bill, screens the patient for retroactive Medicaid eligibility and files the application for them, turning accounts debt buyers would take at 2-4 cents into full Medicaid payments.
customer: County and municipal EMS agencies, their outsourced ambulance-billing companies, and independent ER, anesthesia and radiology physician groups in Medicaid-expansion states. Rural hospitals under 100 beds are the second wave.
problem: Self-pay accounts sit through 90-180 days of statements before they go to an agency or get sold to a debt buyer, and buyers pay only pennies (a few cents on the dollar for medical accounts). Most states let Medicaid reach back only about 3 months before the application date, so by the time a normal collections workflow gives up, the window in which a real payer could have been found has already closed. Patients get dunned for money they may never have owed, and the provider recovers almost nothing.
solution: Take a nightly feed of new self-pay accounts (demographics only, under a BAA). Screen each one for likely Medicaid or charity-care eligibility. Contact the patient in the first two weeks with a simple offer: we complete your Medicaid application for free. Then file the application, chase documents and caseworkers, and bill Medicaid retroactively for the provider. Patients who do not qualify are routed to charity care or a payment plan, and nobody is ever dunned. The firm is paid a contingency on Medicaid dollars actually collected. The dashboard shows each account's days left in the retro window, so providers see the clock that traditional collections ignore.
why_now: The 2025 budget law (OBBBA) cuts Medicaid retroactive coverage to 1 month for expansion adults and 2 months for everyone else, for applications from January 2027. From then on every day of delay burns covered dates, so speed to application becomes the whole product. Providers are also under revenue pressure, states keep passing medical-debt limits that make selling accounts harder, and Medicaid redetermination and work-requirement churn in 2027 makes eligibility-navigation skills scarce and valuable.
revenue_model: 15-20% contingency on Medicaid reimbursements recovered, with an optional $1-2k/month platform fee for charity-care and medical-debt compliance reporting. Ambulance and physician-group accounts are small ($800-$2,500 each) but high in volume and nearly free to service once the screening flow is built.
non_obvious_insight: Collections looks like a persuasion business but is really a timing business. Every step of the traditional workflow (statements, calls, placement at day 120 or later) pushes action past the point where a third-party payer can still be found. Run the workflow backwards, find the payer inside 30 days, and you get the rare collections company that patients thank you for and that pays the provider 10-30x what a debt buyer would.
first_30_days: Pick one expansion state with a 3-month retro window. Hire two ex-hospital eligibility reps and one engineer. Offer 3 county EMS agencies or their billing companies a free back-test of the last 12 months of self-pay accounts, showing how many were eligible and inside a window where enrollment would have paid. Convert the best result into a contingency pilot on new accounts, ideally with an existing certified navigator status. First Medicaid approvals typically land 45-90 days after filing, so signed pilots come in month 1 and cash in months 3-4.

title: CAM and Insurance Pass-Through Audits for Micro-Tenants
one_liner: Read a small tenant's lease, recompute the landlord's annual reconciliation, and dispute overcharges inside the audit window, on contingency.
customer: Restaurants, salons, clinics, gyms and boutiques on NNN or modified-gross leases in strip centers and small retail, typically 1,000-5,000 sq ft.
problem: Landlord reconciliations of common-area, tax and insurance charges are opaque, and pass-throughs rose with property insurance and tax bills (prior knowledge). Audit rights exist in the lease but expire in weeks or months, and owners never read the lease. Rising costs are the top financial challenge for small firms.
solution: Upload the lease and reconciliation. An LLM extracts audit rights, caps, exclusions, gross-up, base year, admin fees and pro-rata share, recomputes the statement, drafts the audit request or dispute letter, calendars deadlines, and escalates to an auditor partner for contested items. Add a renewal-negotiation packet.
why_now: Long-context models read leases cheaply. Enterprise tenants have lease-audit firms, but micro-tenants were never worth the hourly rate.
revenue_model: 25-30% of amounts recovered, with a $99 flat triage fee for leases that show no error.
non_obvious_insight: The lever is the deadline, not the arithmetic. Most owners have never seen their own audit clause, and landlords count on that.
first_30_days: Collect 10 leases and reconciliations through a restaurant association or business improvement district. Run manual audits, measure the hit rate, sign the first contingency deals and refine the extraction.

title: Notice Desk with Contingency Penalty Abatement
one_liner: Snap a photo of any IRS or state notice, get triage and a response, and pay only if the penalty is abated.
customer: 1-25 employee firms, S-corps and small partnerships that received late-filing, payroll-deposit, information-return mismatch or state tax notices.
problem: Notices sit in a drawer or a registered-agent inbox while penalties compound. Abatement routes (first-time abatement, reasonable cause, small-partnership relief) are well established but owners don't know them, and CPAs bill hourly. Filing rules are shifting: the 1099-NEC floor rose to $2,000, 1099-K thresholds reverted, and new tips and overtime reporting will create mismatches. IRS capacity appears strained (prior knowledge).
solution: Forward or photograph the notice. The system classifies it, extracts the deadline and amount, explains the options and drafts the response. An enrolled agent or CPA partner signs, files the abatement request and tracks it. State-notice variants are added by jurisdiction. A $19/month mail-monitoring plan for registered-agent customers catches new notices.
why_now: BOI filing services just lost their main product and need a new recurring hook, and compliance work is moving from filing to interpretation. LLMs can read notices at scale.
revenue_model: 20% of penalties abated, $49 flat for triage on notices with no abatement path, and $19/month monitoring.
non_obvious_insight: A penalty notice is a lead with a known dollar value. Many abatements are near-automatic, so outcome pricing beats hourly billing, and Intuit, Xero and H&R Block cannot easily price on outcomes.
first_30_days: Get 100 anonymized notices from CPA partners and registered-agent companies to train the classifier. Sign an enrolled agent, run 30 abatements sourced from small-business forums, and record the abatement rate.

title: Offline Distilled Agent Box for Denied Networks
one_liner: Ruggedized GPU box that runs small models distilled from a unit's own GenAI.mil agents, with zero connectivity.
customer: National Guard and reserve units, Army and Marine tactical staffs, border and disaster-response agencies, and defense integrators serving units in disconnected or denied environments.
problem: GenAI.mil is unclassified only and needs connectivity, yet users built more than 100k custom agents. The CDAO says compute is the binding constraint, and classified models cannot train in commercial data centers. Units in the field cannot use any of it.
solution: A service that takes a unit's approved agent workflows on GenAI.mil, distills them into small open-weight models with tool wrappers, and ships them on a rugged 1-2 GPU box with a one-screen interface. It updates by sneakernet with signed model bundles.
why_now: Open-weight small models are now good enough for narrow tasks. Right-sizing to cut inference cost is an explicit DoD priority, and model-vendor politics make owning a portable, vendor-independent model attractive.
revenue_model: $40-90K per box and $2-5K per month for update and distillation services. Government pilot funding via SBIR or CSO awards.
non_obvious_insight: The 100k user-built agents are an unwritten requirements document for what warfighters want. The winner distills the demand signal, not the model.
first_30_days: Ask 3 Guard units for one repetitive workflow (maintenance triage, reporting). Build a demo on commodity hardware with an open-weight model. Apply for one SBIR topic and ask an integrator for a paid subcontract.

title: Insurability-at-Close Escrow for Home Listings
one_liner: Listing agents pre-underwrite a house and price the cheapest retrofit fix before listing, so buyers stop discounting for 'uninsurable' uncertainty.
customer: Listing agents, brokerages and sellers in Florida, California and Colorado foothill markets, paying a fee at closing.
problem: Contracts collapse or reprice when buyers cannot get a bindable quote inside the contract window. Homes labeled uninsurable trade to cash buyers at a discount. Much of that discount is uncertainty about fixable issues (roof age, vents, tree clearance), not permanent risk.
solution: A pre-listing 'Insurability File'. Run 3-5 carrier and E&S quotes through a partner agency, then identify the 1-3 cheapest fixes and get contractor quotes. Hold the retrofit cost in escrow at close and give buyers a bindable-quote certificate valid through closing. The buyer gets certainty and the seller gets a closing.
why_now: Citizens has shrunk from about 936K to about 395K policies, so private binding is possible for many Florida homes again. Fannie and Freddie now accept ACV roof coverage (Mar 2026), which opens cheaper insurable paths. Colorado and California rules now credit mitigation.
revenue_model: $750-1,500 per listing at close, plus a 15-25% referral margin on retrofit work and placement commission through the partner agency.
non_obvious_insight: The 'uninsurable' discount is a mispriced-uncertainty premium, and certainty can be bought. Whoever holds the bindable quotes at listing time sets the price.
first_30_days: Pilot with 3 top-producing agents in one Colorado or Florida market. Take 10 stuck or repriced listings, build files by hand, and measure price recovery against comps. Then productize the file template.

title: Code-Upgrade Packages for Home Daycares
angle: Pairing 2: Construction/housing/skilled-trades/home services x Parenting/childcare deserts/Gen Alpha/kids and AI-screens
one_liner: Fixed-price, state-specific remodel packages plus permit navigation that help licensed in-home daycares climb to the next capacity tier, for example 6 to 12 kids.
customer: Licensed family child care providers (capacity 4-8) who want to add slots. Projects are financed by CDFI or SBA microloans, state facility grants, or employers buying slots under the expanded 45F credit.
problem: Family homes are the fastest-growing licensed supply (+4.3% in 2024) versus +1.5% for centers, but growth stalls at capacity thresholds where code and licensing rules jump (egress, fire separation and alarms, second exit, restroom count, fenced yard). Providers face 3-6 agencies (zoning, building, fire, health, licensing) and small builders do not want $6K jobs. The supply map is measured in licensed slots, so this stall is invisible to policy.
solution: Ship a 'capacity ladder' of productized scopes per state (Step 1: 6 to 8 kids, Step 2: 8 to 12). Each has pre-drawn plans, a vetted small-contractor network on fixed prices, and a navigator who files zoning, building, fire and licensing applications. The provider repays from extra tuition, since two added kids at about $1,100/month each pays back a $20K job in roughly 9 months. A financing partner sits on top.
why_now: The 2026 45F credit (40%, or 50% for small businesses, with third-party and pooled arrangements; verify with tax counsel) gives employers a reason to fund slots. The dependent-care FSA rose to $7,500. Remodeling and HVAC slowdowns leave small shops idle and glad to take standardized sub-$10K work. Childcare costs $13,128 a year per child, so any added slot has an immediate paying buyer.
revenue_model: $299-499 code-gap assessment, 12-15% platform fee on each package (typically $6-20K total), permit-navigation fee, and financing referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: Childcare supply is not blocked by demand or by providers' willingness. It is blocked by building-code step functions, which makes it a construction-scoping problem. Each extra licensed slot adds $12-15K a year of revenue at near-zero real-estate cost, far cheaper than the tens of thousands per slot for new center construction.
first_30_days: Pick one state and work through its child-care resource and referral agency to interview 30 providers. Sell 15-20 paid $299 code-gap assessments, catalog the three most common failures, and sign two small contractors to fixed prices. Close the first five packages, using assessment fees to fund the plan sets.

title: Robotaxi Revenue-at-Risk Ratings for Airports and Cities
one_liner: A quarterly exposure index and analyst service that estimates how much airport parking, meter and citation revenue, and the bonds backed by it, will erode as robotaxis scale city by city.
customer: Municipal bond investors and credit research desks, rating and bond insurance analysts, airport and city CFOs and parking operators, and regional lenders holding parking-heavy real estate collateral.
problem: Parking and ground transportation account for roughly 43-45% of airports' non-aeronautical revenue in North America. Waymo now serves Phoenix, San Jose, SFO (curbside) and San Antonio, where a round-trip robotaxi fare of $15-25 undercuts the $30-150 an airport earns on a multi-day parking stay. Cities depend on meters and citations, and garage cash flows collateralize loans. Nobody underwrites this transition; disclosures are scattered across PDFs.
solution: Structure the data from airport financial reports, bond official statements and city ACFRs, then combine it with AV service-area maps, expansion announcements, ride-hail share and ground-transport fee schedules. Publish per-airport and per-city 'percentage of revenue at risk' under three adoption scenarios, plus fee-design advice (AV-specific trip fees, dynamic parking). Ship a free public index to build authority, then sell subscriptions, alerts and consulting.
why_now: Waymo reports 500k paid weekly rides, launched Denver, San Diego and Tampa on September 1 (14 commercial cities), and targets 1M weekly rides by year-end. LAX is already raising per-trip TNC fees to $6. Airports and cities are scrambling for a playbook and investors have no model.
revenue_model: Subscriptions of $12-40k per year for buy-side and rating shops, $25-100k consulting engagements with airports and cities, and custom risk screens for lenders.
non_obvious_insight: The first place AVs bite public finance is not jobs, it is the parking-fee cash flows pledged to bonds that everyone treats as stable. The data is public but unstructured, so a two-person team with careful extraction can build a moat before larger research houses look.
first_30_days: Extract parking and ground-transport revenue lines for the top 30 US airports and 20 cities from public reports. Build a simple three-scenario model and publish a free index and a short note. Send it to 50 muni credit analysts and airport finance officers and sell the first five paid subscriptions.
